title: OCC issues Q2 2025 reports on mortgage performance and bank trading
content: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released two reports for the second quarter of 2025: the Mortgage Metrics Report and the Quarterly Report on Bank Trading and Derivatives Activities. In the Mortgage Metrics Report, 97.5% of first-lien mortgages serviced by large national banks were current and performing at quarter-end, up from 97.3% one year prior. Seriously delinquent mortgages declined year-over-year, with 7,163 new foreclosures initiated—down from the previous quarter but up from the prior year. Loan modifications totaled 8,419, with 94.6% involving multiple affordability-improving actions. In the trading report, U.S. commercial banks and savings associations reported $16.6 billion in trading revenue, a 10.7% increase from Q1 2025. Derivative notional amounts rose 6.2% to $223.5 trillion, with interest rate products making up 66.5% of the total. Four large banks accounted for 87.3% of total industry notional derivatives, and net current credit exposure from derivatives increased to $267 billion.

title: CMBS Distress Rates Decrease Slightly in Q3
content: Commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) distress rates showed a slight improvement in the third quarter of 2025, with overall delinquency rates decreasing to 8.59% in September from 9.44% in August. Special servicing rates declined to 10.63% from 10.95%, resulting in a combined delinquent and/or specially serviced rate of 11.28%, down from 11.78% in August. This metric has remained between 10% and 12% throughout 2025, significantly higher than the sub-5% levels seen in 2022 and 2023, when it peaked at 11.78% in August 2025. Office properties continue to be the most distressed sector, while retail and hotel sectors improved in September, and industrial properties maintained the lowest delinquency rate due to e-commerce demand. Nationally, cap rates rose to 6.4% from 6.3% a year prior, with retail at 7.1% and office at 7.0%. Treasury yields stabilized at 4.18% for the 10-Year as of late September, down from recent highs, and the Federal Reserve’s rate cuts—now in the 4.0% to 4.25% range—have eased borrowing costs. This supports refinancing amid $957 billion in commercial real estate (CRE) maturities in 2025, including $450 billion from banks and $230 billion from CMBS/CLOs. Year-to-date private-label CMBS issuance reached $91.4 billion (up 26% YoY), driven by single-asset, single-borrower loans ($66.9 billion), while agency CMBS surged 39% to $105.7 billion, led by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. CRE CLOs jumped 234% to $22.7 billion, reflecting strong investor demand for yield. Lending shares shifted, with agencies dropping to 20% in H1 2025 (from 25% in 2024) and debt funds/REITs rising to 14%. Total CRE debt outstanding reached $6.2 trillion, with banks holding 49%. Economic indicators show CPI cooling to 2.9% YoY and unemployment at 4.3%. CRED iQ advises investors to stress-test portfolios against upcoming maturities and monitor special servicing transfers, noting that further rate cuts post-October FOMC could widen refinancing windows, but distress resolution remains critical for 2026 stability.

title: Mortgage Refinance Rates Today: October 8, 2025 - Rates Advance Higher
content: On October 8, 2025, mortgage refinance rates across multiple loan types rose slightly. The average rate for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage refinance increased to 6.46%, up 0.61% from the previous week, with an APR of 6.49%. For a $100,000 loan, the monthly principal and interest payment is $629, with total interest over the loan’s life estimated at $127,213. The 20-year fixed refinance average rate rose to 6.11% (APR: 6.14%), resulting in a $723 monthly payment and $73,901 in total interest. The 15-year fixed refinance rate averaged 5.40% (APR: 5.44%), leading to a $812 monthly payment and $46,531 in total interest. Jumbo mortgage refinance rates also increased: the 30-year jumbo rate rose to 6.76% (APR: 6.76%), with a $649 monthly payment on a $100,000 loan; the 15-year jumbo rate jumped to 5.87% (APR: 5.87%), with a $837 monthly payment and $50,904 in total interest. Refinance rates are typically higher than purchase rates due to lender risk, and cash-out refinances carry higher rates than rate-and-term refinances. The refinancing process mirrors a home purchase, requiring similar documentation, appraisals, and closing costs (2% to 6% of the loan amount). Borrowers should compare current and new rates, terms, and balances to estimate savings and calculate the break-even point. Refinancing may be beneficial to lower interest rates, reduce payments, pay off the loan faster, access equity, or eliminate PMI. Experts note that national average rates have remained in the mid-to-high 6% range throughout 2025, with minimal expected movement. Economic factors such as inflation and unemployment may influence future rate trends. The Federal Reserve may cut rates if inflation slows and unemployment stabilizes or rises, potentially lowering mortgage rates. However, if inflation remains high and unemployment falls, rates are likely to stay steady. Homeowners are advised to improve credit scores and make on-time payments to secure better rates when refinancing, and to wait for potential rate decreases rather than acting immediately.

title: Mortgage Rates Today: August 21, 2025 - 30-Year and 15-Year Rates Rise
content: Borrowers will pay more interest this week as the average 30‑year mortgage rate rose to 6.57% from 6.46% a week earlier. The APR on a 30‑year fixed‑rate mortgage is 6.6%, up from 6.49% last week. A $100,000 loan at 6.57% costs about $636 per month in principal and interest and results in $129,870 of total interest over the life of the loan. At a lower rate of 5.53%, the monthly payment would be $819 and total interest $47,859. The average 30‑year jumbo rate increased to 6.7% from 6.67% last week; a $100,000 loan at this rate would cost $645 per month and $132,682 in total interest. Rates have remained in the mid‑to‑high 6% range since late January 2025, while 15‑year rates have hovered between low‑6% and high‑5%. Experts say a significant drop is unlikely soon, though rates could fall if inflation eases or the economy weakens. Mortgage rates follow U.S. Treasury yields and are influenced by Federal Reserve decisions and global events; for example, during the Covid‑19 pandemic the Fed lowered rates, driving mortgage rates to record lows. Home buyers can improve affordability by maintaining a credit score of 670‑850, keeping a debt‑to‑income ratio below 43%, and making a 20% down payment to avoid private mortgage insurance. A 15‑year loan offers lower rates than a 30‑year term if the borrower can afford the higher monthly payment. 'The Federal Reserve's decisions and global events also play a key role in shaping mortgage rates.'

title: Mortgage rates: What the next 5 years may bring
content: The article explains how mortgage rates are linked to the 10‑year Treasury yield and projects future rates for the next five years.  It cites a June 2024 Deloitte forecast that the 10‑year Treasury yield will stay near 4.5% for the rest of 2024, then decline to 4.1% by 2027 and remain there through 2029.  Goldman Sachs analysts agree the yield will hover around 4.1% through 2027, while the Congressional Budget Office projects 4.1% by the end of 2025, 4.0% in 2026 and about 3.9% through 2029.  The article notes that mortgage rates are typically 2.5 percentage points above the Treasury yield, a spread that has widened in recent years (from ~1.5 pp in 2010‑2020 to ~2.6 pp in 2022‑2025).  Using a 2.5 pp spread, a 4.0 % Treasury would imply a 6.5 % mortgage rate; on Sept. 17 the Treasury was 4.06 % and the 30‑year fixed rate was 6.26 %, a 2.2 pp spread.  GPT‑5 suggests a spread of 2.1‑2.3 pp for the next five years.  The forecast therefore projects 2027 mortgage rates around 6.2‑6.4 %.  The article also explains that a 3 % mortgage rate is not expected in the next five years unless a major economic shock occurs, and that rates are unlikely to drop dramatically over the period.  It concludes that choosing a fixed‑rate term should be based on how long a borrower plans to stay in the home.

title: U.S. mortgage loan originations to climb nearly 10% in 2026, iEmergent forecasts
content: iEmergent, a forecasting and advisory services firm for the financial services, mortgage, and real estate industries, has released its 2025–2027 U.S. Mortgage Origination Forecast. The firm projects total mortgage originations will reach $2.27 trillion in 2026, a 13% increase from 2025 and nearly a 10% rise in loan count year-over-year. This growth is driven by a 24% increase in refinance units, fueled by declining interest rates, and a 2.3% increase in purchase units. In 2025, total mortgage originations are forecast to surpass $2 trillion for the first time since 2022, with a 48% jump in refinance dollars and a 12% increase in purchase dollars, representing a 20% overall rise from 2024. By 2027, purchase activity is projected at 4.09 million loans totaling $1.56 trillion, while refinance units are expected to remain steady at 2.37 million, with dollar volume dipping slightly to $754 billion. Mark Watson, iEmergent’s Chief of Forecasting, stated that 'Crossing back above $2 trillion in 2025 signals renewed strength in the mortgage market,' and that 'lower rates and moderating home prices should support activity, though affordability challenges will persist—especially for first-time buyers.' Laird Nossuli, CEO of iEmergent, emphasized that while national trends are important, 'every market will experience the next wave of recovery differently,' and iEmergent’s data provides visibility into market-specific shifts, even down to the census-tract level. The firm’s proprietary forecasting method combines the Purchase Mortgage Generation Rate (PMGR) and the homebuyer pool—households ready, willing, and able to buy a home—using probability theory to estimate loan volumes. iEmergent’s forecasts have proven accurate to within 10 loans in nearly 70% of the nation’s 84,414 census tracts.

title: Current Mortgage Refinance Rates: September 3, 2025 - Rates Climb
content: For September 3 2025, the average 30‑year fixed‑rate mortgage refinance rate was 6.54 %, unchanged from the previous week, with an APR of 6.56 % versus 6.57 % last week. A $100,000 refinance at this rate would cost $635 per month in principal and interest, totaling $129,062 in interest over the life of the loan. The 20‑year fixed rate averaged 6.31 % (APR 6.35 %) and would cost $735 per month, with $76,810 in total interest. The 15‑year fixed rate averaged 5.42 % (APR 5.46 %) and would cost $813 per month, with $46,712 in total interest. Jumbo refinances were slightly higher: the 30‑year jumbo rate fell to 6.69 % (APR 6.69 %) and would cost $645 per month, while the 15‑year jumbo rate was 5.89 % (APR 5.89 %) and would cost $838 per month, with $51,049 in total interest. Lenders typically charge 0.01 %–0.15 % more for a 30‑year refinance than for a purchase loan. Borrowers can lower rates by paying closing costs upfront, buying discount points, or avoiding mortgage insurance. The article advises comparing current rates, balances, and terms to estimate savings and break‑even points. National average rates have hovered in the mid‑to‑high 6 % range since late 2024, with experts predicting minimal movement in the first half of 2025. Forecasts suggest that if inflation slows and unemployment remains stable or rises, the Federal Reserve may cut the federal funds rate, potentially lowering mortgage rates; if inflation stays high and unemployment falls, rates are likely to stay steady. Consequently, those seeking lower rates might wait until later in the year while improving credit scores and payment history to secure the best possible rate.

title: Tassi mutui prima casa: previsioni e consigli per il 2025 e oltre
content: The interest rate on a mortgage is a critical factor, as it significantly impacts the largest cost component of a home loan—interest payments. Even though other costs like notary, insurance, appraisal, and processing fees exist, interest remains the most influential cost determinant. A one percentage point increase on a €200,000, 30-year mortgage can result in thousands of euros in additional repayment. When considering a long-term home loan, it is essential to understand how mortgage interest rates work, including the differences between fixed and variable rates, and to review forecasts for 2025 and beyond to make informed decisions. Two main types of mortgages are fixed-rate and variable-rate. A fixed-rate mortgage locks in the interest rate at the time of contract signing, ensuring the monthly repayment remains constant throughout the loan term, offering financial predictability and protection against rate hikes, though it excludes the benefit of rate decreases. A variable-rate mortgage ties the interest rate to market conditions—such as decisions by the European Central Bank (ECB)—meaning payments rise when rates increase and fall when they drop, making long-term planning more difficult due to potential fluctuations. As of early 2025, after peak rates in 2023–2024, both fixed and variable rates have seen slight declines, with variable rates currently slightly lower than fixed ones. Industry experts express cautious optimism, predicting further rate cuts in the second half of 2025, though uncertainty remains due to ongoing geopolitical complexity and market sensitivity. There is no universally correct choice between fixed and variable rates; currently, variable rates are lower, but this could change in months. The most prudent advice is to consult a professional—such as a tax advisor or a mortgage consultant at one’s bank—before making a decision.

title: Mortgage Rates Today: October 10, 2025 - Rates Stand Still
content: On October 10, 2025, mortgage rates remained stable, with the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 6.39% (APR: 6.42%), down slightly from 6.37% the previous day. The 15-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 5.42% (APR: 5.47%), up from 5.37% the prior week. The 30-year jumbo mortgage rate increased to 6.71% (APR: 6.73%), up from 6.64% last week. For a $100,000 loan, a 30-year fixed mortgage would cost approximately $625 per month in principal and interest, with $125,559 in total interest over the loan’s life. A 15-year fixed mortgage would cost $813 per month, totaling $46,779 in interest. A 30-year jumbo mortgage would require $646 per month, with $132,921 in total interest. Since January 2025, 30-year fixed rates have remained in the mid-to-high 6% range, with a peak of 7.04% in January. Experts do not anticipate significant rate drops in 2025, though decreases may occur in 2026 if the Federal Reserve continues cutting the federal funds rate. Mortgage rates are influenced by the Federal Reserve’s decisions, U.S. Treasury yields, and global economic events. Borrowers can improve their chances of securing lower rates by maintaining a credit score of 670–850, a debt-to-income ratio below 43%, a 20% down payment to avoid private mortgage insurance (PMI), and opting for a 15-year loan term. The APR includes interest, fees, and loan duration, making it a more comprehensive measure of total borrowing cost than the interest rate alone.

title: 2026 Conforming Loan Limits Get Early Boost, But Point to Slowing Home Price Gains - The Truth About Mortgage
content: Three major mortgage lenders—United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), CrossCountry Mortgage, and Rate (formerly Guaranteed Rate)—released 2026 conforming loan limits several months early. The new limits are: $819,000 for one‑unit properties (up from $806,500, a 1.55% increase), $1,048,500 for two‑unit properties (up from $1,032,650), $1,268,000 for three‑unit properties (up from $1,248,150), and $1,575,000 for four‑unit properties (up from $1,551,250). The 1.55% rise is markedly smaller than the 5.2% jump in 2025, when the one‑unit limit moved from $766,550 to $806,500, indicating a slowdown in home‑price growth. UWM explained that the early move "allows brokers to offer larger loan amounts, enabling more borrowers to avoid moving into high‑balance or jumbo loans, which typically come with higher rates and stricter underwriting guidelines." CrossCountry’s COO Jenn Stracensky added that "By raising limits early, our Early Bird Program empowers borrowers to act now and move closer to their dream of homeownership." The article notes that while mortgage rates and home prices can move in the same direction, the modest 1.55% increase suggests affordability pressures may soon curb price appreciation.
